title: Reading and Analysing Literature
summary: Learn to read fiction, poetry and drama closely, write PEEL paragraphs and literary essays, and understand narrative, devices, theme and context.
audience: Secondary and university students of English and literature, and keen readers

body.p: Literature is writing valued for its artistry and its power to show human experience: novels, short stories, poems, plays and oral traditions. Studying it means more than saying what happens. You ask how the writer creates meaning and why it matters. Close reading means reading slowly, noticing word choices, patterns and structure.

steps: Read once for the story or sense: who, where, what happens.
Read again with a pencil: underline words that stand out, repeated images and shifts in tone.
Ask what effect these choices create and what idea they support.

body.p: Original example: 'The market closed early, and the last light leaned on the empty stalls.' The words 'leaned' and 'empty' give the light and the stalls human weight and loneliness. The mood is tired and quiet. A strong note would say: the personification of light creates a lonely, fading atmosphere at the end of the day.

body.tip: Always link a technique to an effect. Naming a device without saying what it does earns few marks.

lessons.title: Narrative: voice, point of view, plot and character

body.p: Narrative is how a story is told. The narrator is the voice that tells it. In first person ('I'), we see events through one character and learn their feelings but may not see the whole truth. In third person limited ('she'), the narrator stays close to one character. In third person omniscient, the narrator knows everything about all characters. An unreliable narrator tells us things we come to doubt.

list: Exposition: setting and characters introduced.
Rising action: events build tension.
Climax: the turning point.
Falling action: consequences unfold.
Resolution: loose ends are settled or left open on purpose.

body.p: Writers may use flashback, foreshadowing (hints of what is coming) or a frame story. Time order is a choice, and it affects suspense.

We learn about characters from what they say, do, think, how others react to them and how the narrator describes them. A round character is complex and changes. A flat character has one main trait. Ask how a character changes and what causes that change.
Poetry packs meaning into few words. Read a poem aloud at least twice. Notice line breaks, pauses and rhythm.

list: Imagery: language that appeals to the senses.
Simile compares using like or as: her voice was like cold water.
Metaphor says one thing is another: the classroom was a beehive.
Personification gives human traits to objects or ideas.
Alliteration repeats starting sounds; assonance repeats vowel sounds.
Enjambment carries a sentence over the end of a line; end-stopped lines pause.
Rhyme and rhythm shape the sound; free verse uses neither in a fixed pattern.

body.p: A sonnet has 14 lines. A haiku has three lines. A ballad tells a story in short stanzas. Oral poetry across Africa, such as praise poems and songs, relies on repetition, call and response, and performance. Form is part of meaning. Ask why the poet chose it, and whether the poem breaks its own pattern at a key moment.

A theme is a central idea that a text explores, such as power, identity, justice, love, migration, tradition and change, or the conflict between the individual and society. A theme is not one word. It is a statement: the text suggests that ambition without conscience destroys people.

list: Notice what repeats: images, symbols, words and situations.
Watch how conflicts are resolved and who is rewarded or punished.
Ask what the ending suggests.

body.p: Setting is time and place and it affects mood and meaning. Context means the social, historical and cultural background of the writer and the story, such as colonialism and independence, war, migration, class or gender roles. Use context to explain choices, but do not replace analysis with a history lesson. Always link back to the text.

body.tip: When you compare texts, compare how each writer treats the same idea, and say why the treatments differ.

body.p: A strong literature essay answers the question with an argument. Start with a thesis: a clear claim that you will prove. Then build each paragraph around a point.

steps: Point: state the idea in your own words.
Evidence: give a short quotation or precise reference.
Explain: analyse how the language or structure creates the effect.
Link: connect back to the question or the next point.

body.p: Example: Point: The writer shows the narrator's isolation. Evidence: 'the last light leaned on the empty stalls'. Explain: The personified light and the word 'empty' suggest a world that has been left behind, which mirrors her loneliness. Link: This sets up her later decision to leave.

list: Retelling the plot instead of analysing.
Long quotations. Use short, precise ones.
Statements like 'the writer uses a metaphor' with no effect explained.
Ignoring the question.

body.p: Plan before you write, with three to four points. Leave time to proofread for spelling, punctuation and paragraphing.

lessons.title: Reading widely, careers and creative practice

body.p: Reading widely builds vocabulary, empathy and understanding of how language works. Try different forms and traditions: African, Caribbean, European, Asian and American literatures, translated work, classic and new, fiction and non-fiction. A reading log of one line per book helps you notice your taste and growth.

list: Write a little every day, even ten minutes.
Show feeling through action and detail instead of naming it.
Read your work aloud to hear awkward rhythm.
Revise: the first draft is raw material.

body.p: Study of literature builds skills in analysis, writing and argument that are used in publishing, journalism, teaching, law, communications, marketing, editing, translation, research and the arts. A degree is common for some of these roles. Many writers also build a portfolio of published pieces.

body.tip: Respect the author's work. Quote with credit, and never copy other people's writing into your own assignments.

options: Reading slowly and noticing language choices, patterns and effects

quiz.q: In the line 'the last light leaned on the empty stalls', which device gives light a human action?
A narrator who says 'I' and whose account we begin to doubt is:
Which part of plot is the turning point?
Hints in a story of what will happen later are called:
'The classroom was a beehive' is a:
A sonnet traditionally has how many lines?
Which is best written as a theme?
options: The text suggests that ambition without conscience destroys people

quiz.q: In the PEEL structure, what does 'E' for Explain do?
options: Analyses how the evidence creates an effect

quiz.q: Which is a common essay mistake?
options: Retelling the plot instead of analysing

quiz.q: What is context in literary study?
options: The page number of a quotation
The social, historical and cultural background of a text
A line ending in a full stop
A sentence running over a line break

quiz.q: What is the best way to use a quotation?
options: Use a short, precise quotation and analyse it
